title: ISC CLASS 11 — Physics | Properties of Fluids Viscosity
description: Subject-wise test on Properties of Fluids Viscosity (Physics) for ISC CLASS 11. 50Q.
subject: isc11-physics

questions.question: Which of the following is the SI unit of the coefficient of viscosity?

options.explanation: Poise is a CGS unit of viscosity, not the SI unit.
Poiseuille is a unit of dynamic viscosity in the CGS system, not the SI unit.
Pascal-second (Pa·s) is the SI unit of the coefficient of viscosity.
dyne-second/cm² is a CGS unit of viscosity, not the SI unit.

questions.explanation: The SI unit of the coefficient of viscosity (η) is Newton-second per square meter (N·s/m²), which is equivalent to Pascal-second (Pa·s). Poise and dyne-second/cm² are CGS units.
questions.hint: Recall that the SI unit for viscosity is derived from force per unit area per unit velocity gradient.
questions.subject: isc11-physics

questions.question: How does the viscosity of a liquid generally change with an increase in temperature?

options.explanation: Viscosity of liquids decreases with an increase in temperature.
Viscosity of liquids decreases with an increase in temperature due to weakened intermolecular forces.
Viscosity of liquids is not constant; it changes with temperature.
Viscosity of liquids decreases monotonically with an increase in temperature.

questions.explanation: For liquids, intermolecular forces (cohesive forces) are responsible for viscosity. As temperature increases, the kinetic energy of molecules increases, weakening these intermolecular forces, and thus reducing the resistance to flow (viscosity).
questions.hint: Consider the effect of temperature on the movement of molecules in a liquid.
questions.subject: isc11-physics

questions.question: According to Newton's Law of Viscosity, the viscous force (F) acting between two layers of a fluid is directly proportional to:

options.explanation: The viscous force is proportional to the area, but not solely dependent on it.

options.text: The velocity gradient (dv/dy) between the layers
options.explanation: The viscous force is proportional to the velocity gradient, but not solely dependent on it.
The viscous force is directly proportional to both the area and the velocity gradient.
The viscous force is directly proportional to both the area and the velocity gradient.

questions.explanation: Newton's Law of Viscosity states that the viscous force F = -ηA(dv/dy), where η is the coefficient of viscosity. This shows that F is directly proportional to both the area A and the velocity gradient (dv/dy).
questions.hint: Refer to the formula for Newton's Law of Viscosity to identify the proportional quantities.
questions.subject: isc11-physics

questions.question: In streamline flow (or laminar flow) of a fluid, the velocity of every particle of the fluid at a given point:

options.explanation: In streamline flow, the velocity at a given point remains constant over time.
In streamline flow, the velocity at a given point remains constant over time.
In streamline flow, the velocity at a given point does not increase with time.
In streamline flow, the velocity at a given point does not decrease with time.

questions.explanation: Streamline flow is characterized by the fact that the velocity of every fluid particle passing through a particular point follows the same path and has the same magnitude and direction as the preceding particle at that point. Thus, the velocity at a given point remains constant over time.
questions.hint: Think about the definition of streamline flow and how it relates to the velocity of fluid particles.
questions.subject: isc11-physics

questions.question: A small spherical ball falls through a viscous liquid. According to Stokes' Law, the viscous force acting on the ball at a given instant depends on:

options.explanation: The viscous force depends on the radius, but not solely on it.
The viscous force depends on the velocity, but not solely on it.

options.text: The coefficient of viscosity of the liquid
options.explanation: The viscous force depends on the coefficient of viscosity, but not solely on it.
The viscous force depends on the radius, velocity, and coefficient of viscosity.

questions.explanation: Stokes' Law states that the viscous drag force F = 6πηrv, where η is the coefficient of viscosity, r is the radius of the sphere, and v is its velocity. Therefore, the viscous force depends on all three factors.
questions.hint: Recall Stokes' Law and identify the variables it depends on.
questions.subject: isc11-physics

questions.question: If two spheres made of the same material but with radii r and 2r fall through a viscous liquid, what will be the ratio of their terminal velocities?

options.explanation: The ratio is not 1:1 because terminal velocity depends on the square of the radius.
The terminal velocity is proportional to the square of the radius, so the ratio is 1:4.
The ratio is not 1:2 because terminal velocity depends on the square of the radius.
The ratio is not 2:1 because the larger sphere has a lower terminal velocity relative to its size.

questions.explanation: The terminal velocity (v_t) of a sphere falling in a viscous liquid is given by v_t = [2r²(ρ - σ)g] / (9η), where r is the radius, ρ is the density of the sphere, σ is the density of the liquid, g is acceleration due to gravity, and η is the coefficient of viscosity. From the formula, v_t is directly proportional to r². So, v_t1 / v_t2 = (r1)² / (r2)² = (r)² / (2r)² = 1/4.
questions.hint: Use the formula for terminal velocity and analyze how it scales with the radius of the sphere.
questions.subject: isc11-physics

questions.question: A metal plate of area 0.02 m² is placed on a liquid layer of thickness 0.01 m. If a force of 0.1 N is required to move the plate with a constant speed of 0.05 m/s, what is the coefficient of viscosity of the liquid?

options.explanation: The calculated value is not 0.1 Pa·s.
The calculated value is not 0.5 Pa·s.
The coefficient of viscosity is calculated to be 1.0 Pa·s.
The calculated value is not 1.5 Pa·s.

questions.explanation: According to Newton's Law of Viscosity, F = ηA (dv/dy). Rearranging the formula: η = F / [A (dv/dy)] = (F × dy) / (A × dv) = (0.1 N × 0.01 m) / (0.02 m² × 0.05 m/s) = 1 Pa·s.
questions.hint: Use Newton's Law of Viscosity to relate the given quantities and solve for the coefficient of viscosity.
questions.subject: isc11-physics

questions.question: A high value of Reynolds number for fluid flow through a pipe generally indicates:

options.explanation: A high Reynolds number indicates turbulent flow, not laminar flow.
A high Reynolds number indicates turbulent flow, not streamline flow.
A high Reynolds number (Re > 3000) generally indicates turbulent flow.
A high Reynolds number does not necessarily indicate steady flow.

questions.explanation: The Reynolds number (Re) is a dimensionless quantity that predicts the flow patterns in different fluid flow situations. For Re > 3000, the flow is generally turbulent.
questions.hint: Recall the significance of the Reynolds number in determining the nature of fluid flow.

questions.question:
**Assertion (A):** The viscosity of liquids decreases significantly with an increase in temperature.
**Reason (R):** The viscous forces in liquids are primarily due to intermolecular cohesive forces, which weaken with increasing kinetic energy of molecules.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
options.explanation: Both the assertion and the reason are true, and the reason correctly explains the assertion.

options.text: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
options.explanation: The reason correctly explains the assertion.

options.text: A is true but R is false.
options.explanation: Both the assertion and the reason are true.

options.text: A is false but R is true.
options.explanation: The assertion is true.

questions.explanation: Both the assertion and the reason are true, and the reason correctly explains the assertion. In liquids, viscosity arises mainly from the cohesive forces between molecules. As temperature increases, the average kinetic energy of the molecules increases, causing them to move further apart and weakening these intermolecular cohesive forces, which in turn reduces the resistance to flow (viscosity).
questions.hint: Evaluate the truth of the assertion and reason separately and determine if the reason correctly explains the assertion.

questions.question: Water flows through a horizontal capillary tube of length L and radius R under a pressure difference P. If the radius is doubled (2R) and the length is halved (L/2), what will be the new rate of flow of water, assuming the pressure difference remains the same?

options.explanation: The new rate of flow is not 4 times the original rate.
The new rate of flow is not 8 times the original rate.
The new rate of flow is not 16 times the original rate.
The new rate of flow is 32 times the original rate due to the changes in radius and length.

questions.explanation: According to Poiseuille's formula, the rate of flow (Q) of a viscous liquid through a horizontal capillary tube is given by Q = (πPR⁴) / (8ηL). If the radius is doubled and the length is halved, the new rate of flow Q2 = 32 * Q1, where Q1 is the original rate of flow.
questions.hint: Use Poiseuille's formula to analyze how changes in radius and length affect the rate of flow.
questions.subject: isc11-physics

questions.question: What is the SI unit of the coefficient of viscosity (η)?

options.explanation: Poise is the CGS unit of viscosity, not the SI unit.
Poiseuille is a unit of dynamic viscosity in the CGS system, not the SI unit.
Pascal-second (Pa·s) is the SI unit of viscosity, equivalent to N·s/m².
N/m² is the unit of pressure or stress, not viscosity.

questions.explanation: The SI unit of viscosity is Newton-second per square meter (N·s/m²), which is equivalent to Pascal-second (Pa·s). Poise is the CGS unit. N/m² is the unit of pressure or stress.

questions.question: With an increase in temperature, the viscosity of liquids generally:

options.explanation: Increasing temperature weakens intermolecular forces, reducing viscosity in liquids.
Increasing temperature does not increase viscosity in liquids.
Viscosity of liquids changes with temperature.
Viscosity of liquids consistently decreases with temperature.

questions.explanation: For liquids, intermolecular forces of attraction (cohesive forces) play a dominant role in viscosity. As temperature increases, the kinetic energy of molecules increases, weakening these intermolecular forces and making it easier for layers to slide past each other, thus decreasing viscosity.
questions.hint: Consider how temperature affects molecular motion and intermolecular forces in liquids.

questions.question: What is the dimensional formula for the coefficient of viscosity (η)?

options.explanation: This is the dimensional formula for momentum, not viscosity.
The dimensional formula for viscosity is [M L⁻¹ T⁻¹].
This is the dimensional formula for energy or work.
This is not the correct dimensional formula for viscosity.

questions.explanation: According to Newton's Law of Viscosity, viscous force F = η A (dv/dx), where F is force, A is area, and dv/dx is the velocity gradient. The dimensional formula is derived as [M L⁻¹ T⁻¹].
questions.hint: Use Newton's Law of Viscosity to derive the dimensions.

questions.question: A small sphere of radius 'r' and density 'ρ' falls under gravity through a viscous liquid of density 'σ' and coefficient of viscosity 'η'. The terminal velocity of the sphere is directly proportional to:

options.explanation: Terminal velocity is proportional to r², not r.
Terminal velocity is inversely proportional to η.
Terminal velocity is directly proportional to the difference in densities (ρ - σ).
Terminal velocity is proportional to r², not 1/r.

questions.explanation: According to Stokes' Law, the terminal velocity (v_t) of a sphere is given by the formula: v_t = [2 r² (ρ - σ) g] / (9 η). From this formula, it is clear that v_t is directly proportional to (ρ - σ), the difference in densities between the sphere and the fluid.
questions.hint: Refer to Stokes' Law for terminal velocity of a sphere in a viscous fluid.

questions.question: A steel ball of radius 1 cm falls through a viscous liquid with a terminal velocity of 10 cm/s. If another steel ball of radius 2 cm falls through the same liquid, its terminal velocity will be:

options.explanation: This would be the case if terminal velocity were proportional to r, not r².
This would imply no change in terminal velocity, which is incorrect.
This would be the case if terminal velocity were proportional to r, not r².
Terminal velocity is proportional to r², so doubling the radius increases terminal velocity by a factor of 4.

questions.explanation: According to Stokes' Law, terminal velocity (v_t) is directly proportional to the square of the radius (r²) of the sphere. Given r₁ = 1 cm, v_t₁ = 10 cm/s, r₂ = 2 cm, v_t₂ = 40 cm/s.
questions.hint: Use the relationship v_t ∝ r² to find the new terminal velocity.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The viscosity of gases increases with an increase in temperature. Reason (R): In gases, viscous forces arise mainly due to the transfer of momentum between layers by molecular diffusion, which increases with temperature.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
options.explanation: Both the assertion and reason are correct, and the reason correctly explains the assertion.

options.text: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
options.explanation: The reason correctly explains the assertion.

options.text: A is true but R is false.
options.explanation: Both the assertion and reason are true.

options.text: A is false but R is true.
options.explanation: The assertion is true.

questions.explanation: For gases, viscosity arises primarily from the transfer of momentum between different layers due to the random motion and collisions of molecules. As temperature increases, the kinetic energy of gas molecules increases, leading to more frequent and energetic collisions and thus a greater transfer of momentum between layers, which results in an increase in viscosity. Both the assertion and reason are correct, and the reason correctly explains the assertion.
questions.hint: Consider the molecular behavior of gases and how temperature affects it.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is necessary for a fluid flow to be considered streamline (laminar) flow?

options.explanation: High velocity tends to promote turbulent flow.
Low velocity and high viscosity favor streamline flow.
This combination tends to promote turbulent flow.
Low viscosity tends to promote turbulent flow.

questions.explanation: Streamline flow occurs when the fluid velocity is below a critical velocity. Higher viscosity tends to promote streamline flow by damping out turbulent eddies, while lower viscosity and higher velocity tend to lead to turbulent flow. Therefore, low velocity and high viscosity favor streamline flow.
questions.hint: Think about the factors that promote smooth, layered flow in fluids.

questions.question: A small oil drop is introduced into a large container of water. The oil drop will tend to become spherical due to:

options.explanation: Viscosity affects the flow of the liquid but does not cause the drop to become spherical.
Density difference affects buoyancy but does not cause the drop to become spherical.
Surface tension minimizes the surface area, causing the drop to become spherical.
Buoyant force affects the motion of the drop but does not cause it to become spherical.

questions.explanation: While viscosity and density differences are relevant to fluid dynamics, the tendency of a liquid drop to assume a spherical shape is primarily due to surface tension. Surface tension minimizes the surface area for a given volume, and a sphere has the minimum surface area.
questions.hint: Consider the forces acting on the oil drop in water.

questions.question: A horizontal plate of area 0.1 m² is separated from a fixed plate by a layer of oil 0.01 m thick. If the coefficient of viscosity of the oil is 0.1 Pa·s, what force is required to move the horizontal plate with a constant speed of 0.1 m/s?

options.explanation: This is too low for the given conditions.
This is still too low for the given conditions.
The calculated force is 1 N.
This is too high for the given conditions.

questions.explanation: According to Newton's Law of Viscosity, the viscous force (F) is given by F = η A (dv/dx). Substituting the values: η = 0.1 Pa·s, A = 0.1 m², dv/dx = 10 s⁻¹, F = 1 N.
questions.hint: Use Newton's Law of Viscosity to calculate the viscous force.

questions.question: Consider two identical spheres, Sphere A and Sphere B, released simultaneously from rest in two different highly viscous liquids. Liquid X has a higher coefficient of viscosity than Liquid Y. Both liquids have the same density, which is less than the density of the spheres. Which statement correctly describes their motion?

options.text: Both spheres will reach the same terminal velocity.
options.explanation: The terminal velocities will differ due to different viscosities.

options.text: Sphere A will reach terminal velocity faster than Sphere B.
options.explanation: Sphere A will take longer to reach its lower terminal velocity.

options.text: Sphere B will reach terminal velocity faster and achieve a higher terminal velocity than Sphere A.
options.explanation: Sphere B will reach its higher terminal velocity faster due to lower viscosity.

options.text: Sphere A will reach terminal velocity faster but achieve a lower terminal velocity than Sphere B.
options.explanation: Sphere A will take longer to reach its lower terminal velocity.

questions.explanation: According to Stokes' Law, terminal velocity (v_t) is inversely proportional to the coefficient of viscosity (η): v_t ∝ 1/η. Since Liquid X has a higher viscosity than Liquid Y (η_X > η_Y), Sphere A (in Liquid X) will experience a greater viscous drag and thus will have a lower terminal velocity compared to Sphere B (in Liquid Y). Also, a higher viscosity means more resistance to motion, so it will take longer to accelerate to the (lower) terminal velocity. Conversely, lower viscosity (Liquid Y) means less resistance, allowing Sphere B to reach its (higher) terminal velocity faster.
questions.hint: Use Stokes' Law to compare the terminal velocities and acceleration times of the spheres.
questions.subject: isc11-physics

questions.question: The SI unit of the coefficient of viscosity (η) is:

options.explanation: Correct. The SI unit of viscosity is Pascal-second (Pa·s).
Poise is the CGS unit of viscosity, not the SI unit.
N/m² is the unit of pressure (Pascal), not viscosity.
This is the CGS unit of viscosity, not the SI unit.

questions.explanation: The coefficient of viscosity (η) is defined by the formula F = ηA(dv/dx), where F is force, A is area, dv/dx is velocity gradient. Therefore, η = F / (A * dv/dx). In SI units, this translates to Newton / (m² * (m/s)/m) = N·s/m². Since N/m² is Pascal (Pa), the SI unit is Pascal-second (Pa·s). Poise is the CGS unit.
questions.hint: Recall the formula for viscosity and derive the SI unit from it.
questions.subject: isc11-physics

questions.question: With an increase in temperature, the viscosity of liquids:

Viscosity does not remain unchanged; it changes with temperature.

questions.explanation: In liquids, viscosity is primarily due to intermolecular cohesive forces. As temperature increases, the kinetic energy of molecules increases, weakening these cohesive forces, and thus reducing the resistance to flow (viscosity).

questions.question: A small sphere is dropped into a tall column of viscous liquid. Which of the following forces acts on the sphere when it achieves terminal velocity?

options.explanation: The sphere experiences more than just the gravitational force.
The sphere experiences more than just the viscous force.

options.text: Gravitational force and viscous force only
options.explanation: The sphere also experiences the buoyant force.

options.text: Gravitational force, buoyant force, and viscous force
options.explanation: Correct. All three forces act on the sphere at terminal velocity.

questions.explanation: When a sphere falls through a viscous liquid, it experiences three forces: the downward gravitational force (weight), the upward buoyant force (due to the displaced fluid), and the upward viscous drag force (opposing motion). At terminal velocity, these forces balance out: Gravitational Force = Buoyant Force + Viscous Force.
questions.hint: Consider all forces acting on the sphere during its motion through the liquid.
questions.subject: isc11-physics

questions.question: According to Stokes' Law, the viscous force (F) acting on a small spherical body of radius 'r' moving with a velocity 'v' through a fluid of viscosity 'η' is given by:

Incorrect. The correct formula is F = 6πηνr.
Correct. This is the formula for viscous force according to Stokes' Law.
Incorrect. This is not the formula for viscous force according to Stokes' Law.

questions.explanation: Stokes' Law states that the viscous drag force on a small spherical body moving through a viscous fluid is directly proportional to its radius, its velocity, and the coefficient of viscosity of the fluid. The constant of proportionality is 6π.
questions.hint: Recall the formula for Stokes' Law.

questions.question: A spherical ball of radius 2 mm is moving through a liquid with a constant velocity of 0.1 m/s. If the coefficient of viscosity of the liquid is 0.5 Pa·s, what is the viscous force acting on the ball?

Incorrect. The calculated value is 3.768 × 10⁻³ N.
Incorrect. The calculated value is 3.768 × 10⁻³ N.
Correct. The viscous force is 3.768 × 10⁻³ N.

questions.explanation: Given: Radius, r = 2 mm = 2 × 10⁻³ m, Velocity, v = 0.1 m/s, Coefficient of viscosity, η = 0.5 Pa·s. According to Stokes' Law, the viscous force F = 6πηνr. F = 6 × 3.142 × 0.5 × (2 × 10⁻³) × 0.1 = 3.768 × 10⁻³ N.
questions.hint: Use Stokes' Law to calculate the viscous force.
questions.subject: isc11-physics

questions.question: A small steel ball is dropped into a long column of glycerine. It is observed that the ball attains a constant velocity after some time. This constant velocity is known as:

options.explanation: Critical velocity is not the term used for this scenario.
Escape velocity is related to gravitational escape, not fluid dynamics.
Correct. The constant velocity is called terminal velocity.
Orbital velocity is related to celestial mechanics, not fluid dynamics.

questions.explanation: When an object falls through a fluid, the viscous drag force increases with its velocity. Eventually, the upward viscous drag force and buoyant force balance the downward gravitational force. At this point, the net force on the object becomes zero, and it falls with a constant maximum velocity called terminal velocity.
questions.hint: Recall the definition of terminal velocity.

questions.question: **Assertion (A):** The rate of flow of a liquid through a narrow tube increases significantly if the radius of the tube is doubled. **Reason (R):** According to Poiseuille's equation, the volume flow rate is directly proportional to the fourth power of the radius of the tube.

This equation clearly shows that the flow rate is directly proportional to r⁴. Therefore, doubling the radius (2r) would increase the flow rate by (2r)⁴ = 16 times, which is a significant increase.

questions.question: Two identical spheres of the same material are dropped from the same height into two different viscous liquids. Liquid A has a viscosity three times that of Liquid B. If the spheres achieve terminal velocities vA and vB respectively, what is the ratio vA/vB?

questions.question: What is the SI unit of the coefficient of viscosity?

options.explanation: Poise is a CGS unit, not the SI unit.
Stoke is the SI unit of kinematic viscosity, not dynamic viscosity.
Pascal-second (Pa·s) is the SI unit of the coefficient of viscosity.
Newton-meter (N·m) is the unit of torque or work, not viscosity.

questions.explanation: The coefficient of viscosity (η) is defined by the formula F = η A (dv/dz), where F is viscous force, A is area, and (dv/dz) is velocity gradient. Rearranging gives η = F / (A * (dv/dz)). Substituting units: N / (m² * (m/s)/m) = N / (m² * s⁻¹) = N s/m². Since Pascal (Pa) is N/m², the SI unit is Pascal-second (Pa·s). Poise is a CGS unit (1 Poise = 0.1 Pa·s).
questions.hint: Recall that the SI unit of force is Newton (N) and the unit of area is square meter (m²).

questions.question: A small spherical ball of radius r falls through a highly viscous liquid with a terminal velocity v. If another ball of the same material but with radius 2r is dropped in the same liquid, its terminal velocity will be:

options.explanation: Terminal velocity is not inversely proportional to radius.
Terminal velocity is proportional to the square of the radius, not directly proportional.
Terminal velocity increases with radius, not decreases.
Since v_t ∝ r², doubling the radius increases the terminal velocity by a factor of 4.

questions.explanation: According to Stokes' law, the terminal velocity (v_t) of a spherical body falling in a viscous liquid is given by v_t = [2 r² (ρ_p - ρ_f) g] / (9 η), where r is the radius of the ball, ρ_p is the density of the ball, ρ_f is the density of the fluid, g is the acceleration due to gravity, and η is the coefficient of viscosity of the liquid. From the formula, v_t is directly proportional to r² (all other factors being constant). So, v_t ∝ r². If the radius is doubled to 2r, the new terminal velocity v' will be proportional to (2r)² = 4r². Therefore, v' = 4v.
questions.hint: Use Stokes' law and note that terminal velocity is proportional to the square of the radius.

questions.question: A small spherical ball of radius 2 mm and density 8 × 10³ kg/m³ is dropped in a long column of liquid of density 1.2 × 10³ kg/m³. If the coefficient of viscosity of the liquid is 0.8 Ns/m², find the terminal velocity of the ball. (Take g = 10 m/s²).

options.explanation: The calculated value is much smaller than this.

The calculated value is much smaller than this.

questions.explanation: The formula for terminal velocity (v_t) of a sphere falling in a viscous liquid is: v_t = [2 r² (ρ_p - ρ_f) g] / (9 η). Given values: r = 2 mm = 2 × 10⁻³ m, ρ_p = 8 × 10³ kg/m³, ρ_f = 1.2 × 10³ kg/m³, η = 0.8 Ns/m², g = 10 m/s². Substituting the values: v_t = [2 × (2 × 10⁻³)² × (8 × 10³ - 1.2 × 10³) × 10] / (9 × 0.8) = [2 × 4 × 10⁻⁶ × 6.8 × 10³ × 10] / 7.2 = [54.4 × 10⁻³] / 7.2 ≈ 0.0755 m/s.
questions.hint: Use Stokes' law for terminal velocity and substitute the given values carefully.
